name: Northern Tutchone
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Northern Tutchone is not in the catalog. The single stress-title item Glottolog attaches to it (Frota & Vigário 2013, Phonology 30.1, a review of the Selkirk Festschrift 'Prosody matters') is a computerized misassignment from the alternate name 'Selkirk' and has nothing to do with the language (Glottolog language code field says so verbatim; Cambridge landing page mentions no Athabaskan language). Beyond the item list I downloaded and read the open YNLC materials (Ritter 1976 Mayo dictionary = Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description; Ritter, McGinty & Edwards 1977 Selkirk noun dictionary = WALS source; 2015 NNDFN dictionary; YNLC alphabet chart; literacy-session TOCs) and the 'Linguistic note' of Legros 1999 via archive.org: all describe a tonal system (two tones high/low in 1976-77, four tones high/mid/low-rising/low in current YNLC orthography and Legros; high tone ~99% predictable on glottal-final syllables) and none says anything about word stress.org, HathiTrust catalog and YNLC directly). Best unread candidates: Rice & Hargus 2005 Introduction to Athabaskan Prosody (paywalled, DOI 10.1075/cilt.269.03ric; medium priority) and Krauss & Golla 1981 HNAI 6 (print only; low). Everything downloaded is with.

tone_statements.quote: By contrast, Tutchone has evolved an elaborate tonal system, at least by Athabaskan standards. In the classification proposed by Krauss, Northern and Southern Tutchone are high- and low-marked respectively, showing either high or low tone on syllables which were earlier closed by glottal stop or (under certain conditions) glottalized consonants. For example, Proto-Athabaskan 'father' *taˀ has reflexes NT -té, ST -tà (often also still with phonetic final glottal closure in both languages), but PA 'stone' *tse· with full open vowel has opposite tonal reflexes, NT tθì, ST (t)θé.

sources.citation: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun / Yukon Native Language Centre (2015). Na-Cho Nyak Dun Northern Tutchone Dictionary (additions from literacy workbooks, July 2015). 43 pp.
sources.quote: The Mayo native language is a tonal language. [...] There are two tones, high tone and low tone. [...] in 99% of cases, a high tone will appear on a syllable which ends with a glottal stop.
sources.note: Silent on stress; reproduces Ritter 1976's tone description in the current orthography (only high tone marked).

sources.citation: Legros, Dominique (1999). Tommy McGinty's Northern Tutchone Story of Crow: A First Nation Elder Recounts the Creation of the World. Mercury Series, Canadian Ethnology Service Paper 133. Hull: Canadian Museum of Civilization. 'Linguistic note'.
sources.quote: The Northern Tutchone alphabet used is adapted from the phonemic chart developed by The Yukon Native Language Centre. It counts 43 consonant sounds [...] and 9 vowel sounds. When vowels are nasalized or lengthened, the meaning changes. [...] Northern Tutchone language has four tones: high, mid, low-rise, and low tone (these are not indicated).
sources.locator: 'Linguistic note' (front matter, before ch. 1; scanned the text)
sources.note: Silent on stress; only notes four lexical tones and contrastive vowel length/nasalization.

sources.citation: Ritter, John, Tommy McGinty & Johnson Edwards (1977). The Selkirk Indian Language Noun Dictionary. Whitehorse: Yukon Native Languages Project, Council for Yukon Indians. (WALS source for Tutchone [tut])
sources.quote: The Selkirk Indian Language is tonal. By "tonal" we mean that the pitch or melody of the words is very important, and great care must be taken to make sure that each syllable is pronounced with the right "accent". There are two tones, high and low. [...] The point here is: the syllable pitches, or tones, are just as important to the make-up of words as are the vowels and consonants. Now in some cases this syllable tone can be predicted.
sources.note: Silent on word stress; 'accent' here means pitch/tone. Minimal pairs given (uts'at 'her forehead' LL vs uts'át 'her womb' LH; thí' 'dog salmon' vs tthì 'rock'); high tone predictable on glottal-final syllables. Same text as Ritter 1976 for the Selkirk (Pelly Crossing) dialect.

sources.citation: Ritter, John (1976). Mayo Indian Language: Dictionary. Whitehorse: Yukon Native Languages Project / Government of the Yukon Territory, Dept. of Education. 134 pp. (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description for nort2941, id 41621, listed by Glottolog as a dictionary)
sources.quote: The Mayo Indian language is a tonal language. This means that the pitch or "melody" of the words is very important, and great care must be taken to make sure that each syllable is pronounced properly. There are two tones, high tone and low tone. [...] in 99% of cases, a high tone will appear on a syllable which ends with a glottal stop. [...] Even this doesn't tell the whole story, however, because high tone can also occur on syllables which don't end with a glottal stop, as in dàn tthíyé' where the second syllable doesn't have a glottal stop.
sources.note: Silent on word stress. Describes a two-tone (high/low) system; high tone largely predictable from a syllable-final glottal stop, otherwise lexical. No word for stress/accent-placement anywhere in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: no 'stress').

sources.citation: Yukon Native Language Centre (n.d.). Northern Tutchone Alphabet (YNLC orthography chart, 2 pp.)
sources.quote: Low tone vowels are unmarked. Example u. High tone vowels are indicated with an acute accent over the vowel. Example ú. Mid tone is marked with a macron (bar) over the vowel. Example ā. Low-rising tone is indicated with a caron (hachek) over the vowel. Example ǎ.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Current YNLC orthography marks four tones (low, high, mid, low-rising), i.e. more than the two of Ritter 1976/1977.

sources.note: Tutchone section pp. 78-79: 'Vowel constriction has developed into tone, but the system differs in the two dialects. In Northern Tutchone constricted vowels develop high tone (as in Kaska and Slavey-Hare); in Southern Tutchone, low tone (as in Tagish and Tahltan).' sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. (1979 [2003 revision]). Athabaskan Tone. Ms., Alaska Native Language Center, 72 pp. ANLA item CA961K1978 (published with light editing as Krauss 2005, in Hargus & Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody, 55-136).
sources.note: Northern Tutchone is a high-marked tone language: 'The acute or high-marked area includes Chipewyan, Beaver, Slave, Kaska, Northern Tutchone, Hare-Bearlake-Mountain, and also Chilcotin' (p. 11); 'Northern Tutchone shows quite regular high-marked correspondences. In 25 of 26 instances of CVC(') it has high tone, and in all 24 instances of CV)C it has low' (p. 58); data source Ritter et al. 1977 (p. 15). Stress is discussed only for toneless/poorly known languages (Tsetsaut, Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai, PCA, Carrier); nothing on Tutchone stress.

tone.says: Sets tone aside: the syllable-structure section states that nasality and tone are represented on separate (autosegmental) tiers and the rest analyses only segmental rhymes (nucleus + coda charts for Upper and Lower Northern Tutchone, vowel inventories N /a e o i u/ vs S /a e/, [ʌ] = /e/, development of PA stem rhymes *i *e *u *a *a' *ʊ by coda class, orthography recommendations). No tone inventory, no tone rules, nothing on stress.
